title: SSLs.com Review 2026: Pricing, Setup & Is It Worth It?
headings: Why This Matters More in 2026 Than It Used To
DV vs. OV vs. EV: Which Tier Do You Actually Need?
text: Every ecommerce store you launch lives or dies on trust signals, and the padlock icon in a shopper’s address bar is one of the cheapest trust signals you can buy. If you are still weighing what high-ticket dropshipping actually requires before you open a storefront, an SSL certificate belongs on that checklist right next to picking a supplier and registering your business. SSLs.com is a budget SSL certificate reseller that has been selling Sectigo and Comodo-brand certificates since roughly 2009 out of Phoenix, Arizona. We put it through a full review for 2026, covering pricing, setup, support, and how it stacks up against the handful of competitors an entrepreneur is likely to consider instead. You can browse the full Ecommerce Paradise resource library for the rest of the store-launch checklist while you read. What Is SSLs.com? SSLs.com is a reseller, not a certificate authority. It buys certificates in bulk from Sectigo (the CA formerly known as Comodo CA) and resells them at a discount versus buying directly from Sectigo’s own storefronts. That structure is exactly how most budget SSL providers operate, and it is not a red flag by itself. What matters is whether the certificate you get is identical to the one you would get anywhere else that resells the same Sectigo root, and it is. The browser padlock does not know or care which reseller sold you the certificate. One mix-up worth clearing up before you buy anything: SSLs.com (with an “s”) is a completely different company from SSL.com (no “s”), which is its own certificate authority based in Houston, Texas. Review aggregators and even directories occasionally conflate the two, so double-check the URL before you compare pricing or read reviews, since a review of one tells you nothing about the other. Bottom line: if you want the cheapest possible way to get a browser-trusted padlock on a store or landing page without paying for extras you do not need, SSLs.com is worth a look before you default to whatever your host tries to upsell you. SSLs.com Pricing in 2026 SSLs.com’s pricing moves around with promotions, so treat these as a directional snapshot rather than a locked-in quote. Single-domain PositiveSSL (domain-validated) certificates have been listed from roughly $3.75 per year, with occasional promo pricing dipping into the $2.50 to $3 range. The higher-warranty Comodo EssentialSSL single-domain option runs from around $11.89 per year. Multi-domain PositiveSSL certificates covering three domains start near $17.88 per year, and PositiveSSL Wildcard certificates, which cover a domain plus all of its first-level subdomains, run roughly $32.88 to $39.99 per year depending on the current promotion. At the top end, Comodo PremiumSSL Wildcard lists from about $112.99 per year and Comodo EV Multi-Domain SSL from around $69.99 per year. Those numbers put SSLs.com well below what you would pay buying the equivalent certificate directly from Sectigo, which prices its own single-domain DV certificate from about $110 per year. That gap exists because Sectigo’s direct storefront is built for enterprise buyers, not solo entrepreneurs shopping for the cheapest valid certificate. Setting Up a Certificate The purchase flow is standard for a Sectigo reseller: pick a certificate type, generate a certificate signing request (CSR) from your server or hosting control panel, submit it through SSLs.com’s dashboard, complete domain validation (usually an email confirmation or a DNS/file-based check), and download the issued certificate to install. If your store runs on Shopify, WooCommerce through a managed host, or most modern hosting panels, you likely will not touch a CSR at all, since the host handles certificate issuance automatically and a reseller-purchased certificate is really only worth buying when you are running your own VPS or dedicated server outside of that managed flow. SSLs.com’s dashboard walks through CSR generation for the most common server types, which is helpful if you are self-managing infrastructure for the first time. Support tends to route through a ticket system rather than live chat, so expect a delay of a few hours for anything beyond documentation you can find yourself. Worth knowing before you start: if you are running any kind of custom checkout or self-hosted store infrastructure, budget an extra 20 to 30 minutes for the CSR and validation steps the first time through. Longer certificate terms typically lock in the current promo rate, so it is worth deciding on a term length before you check out rather than defaulting to whatever is preselected. Certificate Types at a Glance Certificate Type Starting Price Best For PositiveSSL (single domain) ~$3.75/yr A single store or landing page Comodo EssentialSSL ~$11.89/yr Higher warranty on one domain PositiveSSL Multi-Domain ~$17.88/yr Several unrelated domains PositiveSSL Wildcard ~$32.88 to $39.99/yr A domain plus unlimited subdomains Comodo EV Multi-Domain ~$69.99/yr A registered business wanting extended validation Prices reflect promotional listings observed in 2026 and fluctuate, so confirm the current rate at checkout rather than treating any of these as a fixed quote. Installing on Different Platforms How much of this process you actually touch depends entirely on where your store lives. Shopify, BigCommerce, and most fully hosted platforms issue and auto-renew certificates for you at no extra charge, which means a reseller-purchased certificate is redundant on those platforms rather than an upgrade. Self-managed WooCommerce installs on shared or managed hosting often get free certificates through the host’s own Let’s Encrypt integration, so check your host’s control panel before buying anything separately. Where a purchased SSLs.com certificate genuinely earns its keep is on a bare VPS, a dedicated server, or any environment where you are handling web server configuration yourself and want a longer-lived, higher-warranty certificate than the free automated options provide. Trust, Refunds, and Support Quality SSLs.com carries an “Excellent” rating on Trustpilot in the 4.3 to 4.5 out of 5 range across roughly a thousand reviews, and a 4.5 out of 5 rating on G2. Those numbers put it comfortably in line with other budget SSL resellers, though nowhere near flawless. Recurring complaints in lower-starred reviews center on support response time rather than the certificates themselves failing to work. For comparison, independent reviewer TechRadar has covered several competing SSL and domain providers in the same budget category, and the pattern holds across the space: ticket-based support is the norm at this price point, not the exception, so it is not a reason to rule SSLs.com out specifically. On refunds, SSLs.com’s own knowledge base states you can request a refund within 90 days of purchase if the certificate has not yet been issued, or within 15 days of issuance if it has already been activated. Refunds are issued as account credit rather than a reversal to your original payment method. That is a meaningfully more generous pre-issuance window than the “30-day money-back guarantee” language you will still see repeated in some older reviews, which appears to describe an outdated version of the policy rather than what is currently published. We could not independently confirm SSLs.com’s exact warranty dollar figure for a given certificate tier, so if warranty coverage matters for your use case, confirm the current number on the product page before you buy rather than relying on any secondhand figure, including ours. Why This Matters More in 2026 Than It Used To Two changes make SSL certificate management more of a recurring task than a one-time checkbox this year. First, the CA/Browser Forum’s ballot SC-081v3 phased down maximum certificate validity. As of March 15, 2026, new certificates are capped at 200 days instead of the 398-day maximum that had been standard since 2020, with further cuts to 100 days in 2027 and 47 days by 2029. That means whatever certificate you buy now, you are renewing sooner than you would have a year ago, and automation is becoming less optional over time. Second, Google’s Chrome browser began rolling out an “Always Use Secure Connections” default in 2026 , warning visitors before they load a site over plain HTTP, with full rollout to all users landing in October. A store still running on HTTP is about to become a lot more visible to shoppers as unsafe, not just quietly unranked. Neither change is specific to SSLs.com, but they both raise the cost of letting a certificate lapse or skipping HTTPS on a secondary domain, which is exactly the kind of oversight a cheap, fast-issuing reseller like this one is built to prevent. DV vs. OV vs. EV: Which Tier Do You Actually Need? According to DigiCert’s own explainer , a domain-validated (DV) certificate only confirms you control the domain, which is fast and cheap but confers no business-identity assurance. Organization-validated (OV) certificates add roughly nine verification checks confirming your registered business is real, and extended-validation (EV) certificates go further with around sixteen checks including a phone call confirming your employment at the company. For most single-store ecommerce sites, a DV certificate is genuinely sufficient, since modern browsers no longer display the old green-bar visual treatment that once made EV certificates stand out to shoppers. Save the OV or EV upgrade for a checkout domain tied to a registered business entity where the extra verification has some practical value beyond the certificate itself. SSLs.com vs. the Alternatives, Briefly We cover the full head-to-head breakdown in our SSLs.com alternatives guide , but here is the short version. Namecheap sells effectively the same underlying Comodo and Sectigo certificates from around $5.99 per year. It is wrapped into a much larger domain and hosting ecosystem, which is convenient if you already manage domains there. GoDaddy advertises promotional pricing as low as $5.99 per month on a multi-year term. Independent reviews from TechRadar put its standard, non-promotional pricing closer to $69.99 per year, well above SSLs.com. If you want a broader brand catalog that includes DigiCert and GeoTrust certificates alongside Sectigo, TheSSLStore is the more direct reseller-to-reseller competitor. Its cheapest DV certificate starts higher, around $16 per year, but the extra brand selection can matter for agencies managing certificates across many client domains. Our take: for a single-domain DV certificate on a lean ecommerce budget, SSLs.com’s current pricing is difficult to beat among the resellers we compared it against. How Renewal Actually Works Because certificate lifespans are shrinking industry-wide rather than staying at the old 398-day standard, renewal is worth planning for rather than discovering the hard way when a browser starts flagging your checkout page as insecure. SSLs.com sends renewal reminder emails ahead of expiration, but relying solely on an inbox notification is risky if that address changes or the email lands in spam. The more durable fix is to set a calendar reminder tied to your certificate’s actual issuance date, or, if you are comfortable with basic server administration, to move toward an automated renewal tool like ACME or Certbot for any certificate type that supports it. Automated renewal is already the default expectation for free certificates issued through Let’s Encrypt, and as the CA/Browser Forum’s phase-down continues toward a 47-day maximum validity by 2029, manual renewal on a purchased certificate is going to become impractical for anyone managing more than a handful of domains. Building that habit now, while renewal windows are still measured in months rather than weeks, saves you from a scramble later. If your store spans multiple domains or subdomains, this is also the point where a wildcard or multi-domain certificate starts paying for itself: one renewal cycle to track instead of five separate ones scattered across your calendar. Pros and Cons What works in SSLs.com’s favor: genuinely low per-year pricing on DV and wildcard certificates, a wide range of Sectigo/Comodo certificate types in one dashboard, a refund window that is actually more generous than the outdated “30-day” figure floating around online, and issuance that is typically fast enough to finish same-day for a DV certificate. Where it falls short: support is ticket-based rather than live chat or phone, the catalog is limited to one certificate authority family rather than the broader multi-brand catalog a reseller like TheSSLStore offers, and published warranty figures for specific tiers were not something we could confirm independently, which means you should verify that detail yourself if it factors into your decision. Who Should Buy From SSLs.com If you are running a self-hosted store, a VPS, or any setup where you are manually managing certificates rather than relying on automatic issuance through your host or platform, SSLs.com is a reasonable default for keeping costs down while staying fully browser-trusted. If your store already gets SSL handled automatically through Shopify, a managed WooCommerce host, or a similar platform, you likely do not need to buy a certificate from anyone at all. The money is better spent elsewhere in the business, starting with the fundamentals covered in our guide to choosing a niche . Once the niche is locked in, getting your business entity set up correctly matters more to your long-term margins than which SSL reseller you choose. Ready to lock in a certificate? See SSLs.com’s current plans and pricing and pick the term length that matches how long you plan to run the current infrastructure before a redesign or migration. Frequently Asked Questions Is SSLs.com the same company as SSL.com? No. SSLs.com (with an “s”) is a Phoenix-based reseller of Sectigo and Comodo certificates. SSL.com (no “s”) is a separate, Houston-based certificate authority. They are frequently confused but are unrelated businesses. Do I need to buy a certificate from SSLs.com if I run my store on Shopify? No. Shopify and most managed platforms issue and renew SSL certificates automatically at no extra cost. A reseller-purchased certificate matters mainly for self-hosted stores or custom server setups. How long does SSLs.com certificate issuance take? Domain-validated certificates typically issue within minutes to a few hours after you complete domain validation. Organization- and extended-validation certificates take longer because they require manual business verification. What is SSLs.com’s refund policy? Per SSLs.com’s own knowledge base, refunds are available within 90 days of purchase if the certificate has not yet been issued, or within 15 days of issuance if it has, credited to your account rather than refunded to your original payment method. Is a cheap DV certificate good enough for an ecommerce checkout page? For encryption purposes, yes. A DV certificate encrypts the connection identically to a more expensive OV or EV certificate. The higher tiers add business-identity verification, not stronger encryption, and their visible trust signals to shoppers have diminished as browsers phased out special EV styling. Why do SSL certificates expire so much faster now than they used to? The CA/Browser Forum’s industry-wide ballot phased maximum validity down from 398 days to 200 days as of March 2026, with further reductions scheduled through 2029, largely to push the industry toward automated certificate renewal and reduce the window a compromised certificate can stay valid.
